Task 1: Getting started with the Astronaut Database

The data this week comes from Mariya Stavnichuk and Tatsuya Corlett.

This article talks about the data set in greater detail.

This database contains publically available information about all astronauts who participated in space missions before 15 January 2020 collected from NASA, Roscosmos, and fun-made websites. The provided information includes full astronaut name, sex, date of birth, nationality, military status, a title and year of a selection program, and information about each mission completed by a particular astronaut such as a year, ascend and descend shuttle names, mission and extravehicular activity (EVAs) durations.

You can use the data set directly by importing the csv file in the repository.

  1. Create a new data set total_hours_df containing the unique names and the total duration of all missions in hours (total_hrs_sum) for each astronaut in the data. Then, visualize the distribution of that variable using an appropriate plot type.
total_hours_df <- astronauts |>
  group_by(name) |>
  summarise(
  total_hrs_sum = sum(hours_mission, na.rm = T) 
  )

head(total_hours_df)
ggplot(total_hours_df, aes(x = total_hrs_sum)) +
  geom_histogram() +
  labs(
    x = "Total mission hours",
    y = "Number of astronauts",
    title = "Distribution of Total Mission Hours"
  )

  ) +
  theme_minimal()


Task 2 – Writing functions

  1. Given a vector of birthdates, write a function that computes the vector of corresponding ages in years.
get_ages <- function(year_of_birth) {
  current_year <- as.numeric(format(Sys.Date(), "%Y"))
  current_year - year_of_birth
}

#  test:
get_ages(c(1934, 1935, 1921))
[1]  92  91 105


  1. Write both_na(), a summary function that takes two vectors of the same length and returns the number of positions that have an NA in both vectors. For example the two vectors a <- c(1, NA, 2, NA) and b <- c(3, NA, NA, 4) should give 1.
  a <- c(1, NA, 2, NA)
  b <- c(3, NA, NA, 4)
  both_na <- function(a, b) {
    sum(is.na(a) & is.na(b))
  }

# Test the function
both_na(a, b)
[1] 1


  1. Program a function check_password(pw) that takes a password string pw and returns a funny strength rating according to the following rules:
  1. If the password contains the word "password" (in any mix of upper/lower case), return "Terrible!".
  2. If the password is shorter than 6 characters, return "Too weak".
  3. If it contains only letters, return "Meh".
  4. If it contains letters and numbers, return "Not bad".
  5. If it contains letters and numbers and at least one special character from !@#$%^&*?, return "Strong".

Write the function and test it with at least five different passwords that trigger different outputs. Also, use functions from the stringr package to execute the checks in your function (hint: look up str_detect() and str_length()).

library(stringr)

check_password <- function(pw) {
  
  if (str_detect(pw, regex("password", ignore_case = TRUE))) {
    return("Terrible!")
  }
  
  if (str_length(pw) < 6) {
    return("Too weak")
  }
  
  
  if (str_detect(pw, "[a-zA-Z]") && str_detect(pw, "[0-9]") && str_detect(pw, "[!@#$%^&*?]")) {
    return("Strong")
  }
  
  if (str_detect(pw, "[a-zA-Z]") && str_detect(pw, "[0-9]")) {
    return("Not bad")
  }
  

  if (str_detect(pw, "^[a-zA-Z]+$")) {
    return("Meh")
  }
  
  return("Uncategorized")
}


passwords <- c("PassWORD123", "abc12", "SecretPass", "Secret123", "Secret123!")


sapply(passwords, check_password)
PassWORD123       abc12  SecretPass   Secret123  Secret123! 
"Terrible!"  "Too weak"       "Meh"   "Not bad"    "Strong"
